climbing_route.label: Sitkum Glacier to the 9,500 ft saddle
climbing_route.notes: From Boulder Basin (~5,700 ft) go cross-country and onto glacier: head southeast onto the toe of the Sitkum Glacier, staying in the corridor left (north) of the rock rib/icefall that splits the lower glacier, then trend northeast up-glacier to a broad saddle at approximately 9,500 ft immediately east of Sitkum Spire. Real crevasse hazard in both the lower and upper sections — rope up for glacier travel, carry standard crevasse-rescue gear, and expect more open crevasses by late summer. Route-finding on the broad, featureless summit plateau and glacier can be tricky in flat light or whiteout; a GPS track or careful compass bearing is worthwhile.

climbing_route.label: Summit ridge scramble from the saddle
climbing_route.class: class 2-3 with a class 3-4 step near the top
climbing_route.notes: A short, loose pumice-and-rock ridge scramble leads from the saddle to the summit block of Sitkum Spire itself.

wa_south_spur.skip_reason: The approach text describes only the walk in — Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack River ford, the Easy Ridge climbers' trail, the Imperfect Impasse workaround, and the alternate low-orbit traverse — all of it ending at the Perfect Pass high camp. The Class 4 rock step it names is on the Easy Ridge approach before high camp, not on the South Spur, and the spur's own climbing above the south-side snowfields is never described.

climbing_route.label: Gully/couloir below the tower
climbing_route.class: class 3-4 slabs on the alternate entry
climbing_route.notes: Entered off the top of the Quien Sabe Glacier after a roped traverse east several hundred feet. If a bergschrund or seracs bar the direct line, class 3-4 slabs on the left provide an alternate entry, rejoining the couloir about 100 ft up. Getting into the correct gully matters: on July 10, 2005 a six-person Mountaineers party mistakenly climbed a similar-looking but incorrect gully here; during the roped traverse back toward the standard line a climber was struck by rockfall, and minutes later, during the retreat rappel, a natural boulder anchor gave way, killing three and seriously injuring a fourth. Confirm the line (ideally with GPS track or beta photos) before committing, especially in poor visibility.

climbing_route.label: First two pitches of the Southeast Ridge
climbing_route.notes: There is no separate approach line to the Southeast Face itself — parties climb the first two pitches of the Southeast Ridge (the block/dihedral pitch to the notch, described in that route).

climbing_route.label: Rappel to the base of the Southeast Face crack pitch
climbing_route.notes: Rappel from a fixed anchor at the top of pitch 2 of the Southeast Ridge to reach the base of the Southeast Face's crack pitch.

climbing_route.label: Talus and snow to the col east of the summit block
climbing_route.notes: From the Thunder Basin camp the route continues across talus and snow to a col east of the summit block; ice axe and crampons are typically needed for the sometimes-firm snow.

climbing_route.label: Loose gully on the left, about 85 ft to a ledge system
climbing_route.notes: Climbs a loose gully on the left for about 85 ft to a ledge system. Rock in the gully is loose — helmet up and manage rope/party spacing to avoid dropping rock on others below.

climbing_route.label: Broken chimney/face pitch to the summit
climbing_route.class: Class 4 to easy Class 5 depending on conditions
climbing_route.notes: A broken chimney/face pitch leads from the ledge system to the summit. Rock in the chimney is loose, so helmet up and manage rope/party spacing to avoid dropping rock on others below.

climbing_route.label: South Couloir from 4,000-4,300 ft
climbing_route.notes: Ascend the couloir a few hundred feet — firm snow in early season, loose scree by mid/late summer — then exit onto its west side and continue up scree to about 5,000 ft.

climbing_route.label: Ascending rightward traverse to the spur crest
climbing_route.notes: From about 5,000 ft, make an ascending rightward traverse below cliff bands to reach the crest of a semi-open spur, then work up and right to the base of 'the Hourglass'.

climbing_route.label: The Hourglass
climbing_route.notes: A narrow rock/snow constriction and the technical crux of the approach to the summit block: Class 3 scrambling, or a steep 35-45° snow climb in early season requiring an axe and solid self-arrest skills. Watch for a moat opening at its base as the snow recedes.

climbing_route.label: 'Dwarf door' notch and the final gully to the south summit
climbing_route.class: Class 4 for the last roughly 200 vertical feet
climbing_route.notes: Above the Hourglass continue on scree or snow toward the summit ridge and watch closely for a cairned, easy-to-miss notch on the right — climbers describe it as a 'dwarf door', nearly invisible until you're directly in front of it. That notch is the route-finding key to the final gully leading to the true south summit, the last roughly 200 vertical feet of which is Class 4 with real exposure. No reliable water above camp on the scree/couloir — plan on snowmelt or carrying water.

climbing_route.label: Short exposed rock step past Tin Can Gap
climbing_route.notes: Some parties fix or find a hand-line/rope on a short exposed rock step just past Tin Can Gap, before the glacier — treat it as unverified fixed gear.

climbing_route.label: Queest-Alb (Three Fingers) Glacier crossing
climbing_route.notes: Beyond Tin Can Gap, drop off-trail onto the glacier — a short but real crossing with a moat between ice and rock that widens through the season. Crampons and axe strongly recommended, especially before August; a rope is worth carrying if crevasses are open.

climbing_route.label: Rock and snow scramble to the ladders
climbing_route.notes: On the far side of the glacier, scramble up rock and snow past the base of the summit block to the historic lookout's ladder system.

climbing_route.label: Three fixed wooden ladders to the lookout deck
climbing_route.notes: Three fixed wooden ladders bolted/pinned into the rock, stacked in sequence, gain the final rock band to the lookout deck. The transition between the second and third ladder is the trickiest move and is awkward with a full pack; exposure is significant and a slip here would be serious, which is why this last pitch makes the route a scramble rather than a hike despite no rope typically being used.

climbing_route.label: West along the Rampart Ridge crest from the 5,570 ft saddle
climbing_route.notes: From the saddle, turn west and follow the increasingly exposed climber's path along the ridge crest toward Alta's summit block, negotiating three false summits, class 2-3 rock steps, and short sections of real exposure. WTA and trip reports flag a section where the path skirts a cliff edge — fall consequences are serious here, and the route should not be attempted with snow on the ridge.

climbing_route.label: Final ridge scramble to the 6,274 ft summit
climbing_route.notes: A helmet is commonly recommended for the final ridge scramble due to loose rock and exposure.

climbing_route.label: 'Vertical snow wall' step at the 5,550 ft notch
climbing_route.notes: The main gully/talus slope tops out at the notch (~5,550 ft) between South Baring and the main (true) summit; this gully and the basin below hold snow late into the season, so an ice axe (and possibly crampons) are recommended into mid-summer. The step right at the notch is sometimes called the 'vertical snow wall,' and its difficulty varies year to year with snowpack.

climbing_route.label: Boulder and heather to the summit block
climbing_route.notes: From the notch, scramble up and right a short distance, break out onto an open slope, then trend left/north across class 2-3 boulder and heather terrain toward the base of the summit block. A helmet is recommended from the boulder field onward given loose rock.

climbing_route.label: Summit block, left (west) side
climbing_route.notes: Climb the summit block on its left (west) side via class 3-4 moves to reach the true 6,127 ft summit.
